# Abstract

Between the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 and the collapse of the Third Reich in 1945, the population of Europe outside the Soviet Union together with Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland rose from 342,57M to a pre-war peak of 396,37M in 1939 before falling by 11,63M (-2,9%) to 384,74M by 1945. Across the 7.148.884,3 km² domain (4.970.091,5 km² excluding the North Atlantic islands and the Greenland ice sheet), mean overall density increased from 47,92 inhabitants/km² in 1914 to 55,44 inhabitants/km² in 1939 and receded to 53,82 inhabitants/km² in 1945; excluding the North Atlantic sub-region, continental and insular European density climbed from 68,9 to 79,72 before slipping to 77,37 inhabitants/km². This 31-year span witnessed the sharpest demographic shocks in modern European history: First World War military and civilian mortality, the 1918–1919 influenza pandemic, post-imperial border revisions and compulsory population exchanges under the Versailles, Saint-Germain, Trianon and Lausanne settlements, rapid inter-war fertility decline across industrialised western and central Europe, the Spanish Civil War and Republican exile, Second World War combat and civilian slaughter, the industrialised genocide of the Holocaust and the initial wave of 1945 post-war border shifts and expulsions across the Oder-Neisse line, East Prussia and the Sudetenland. Whereas non-belligerent Iberia expanded by 32,7% across 1914–1945 and the North Atlantic by 48,8%, Poland contracted by 25,5% (-8,17M) between 1939 and 1945 alone and Czechoslovakia and Hungary fell by 10,7% (-2,55M). MAGNETIC harmonises these trajectories across 11 fixed sub-regional masks anchored against 1.149 scraped inter-war historical GIS sub-administrative enumerations and a 10.046-settlement urban gazetteer spanning 45 modern states and territories.

# Background

## Europe on the Eve of 1914

In the summer of 1914 Europe outside the Russian Empire stood near the zenith of its nineteenth-century demographic expansion. A century of declining mortality, railway integration, steamship grain imports and industrial urbanisation had lifted the 11 sub-regions of this study to 342,57M inhabitants [@Mitchell2007; @RosesWolf2019]. Yet the continent was no longer demographically uniform. Industrialised north-western and central Europe already exhibited the advanced phase of the first demographic transition: marital fertility had been falling in France since the late eighteenth century and across Britain, Germany, Belgium, Switzerland and Scandinavia since the 1870s and 1880s [@CoaleWatkins1986; @Dupaquier1988; @WrigleySchofield1981]. By contrast, agrarian southern and eastern Europe—Spain, Portugal, southern Italy, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, Serbia and Albania—retained crude birth rates above 30 to 40 per thousand alongside rapidly falling death rates, generating formidable cohorts of young adults despite mass transatlantic emigration.

Population density reflected this industrial divide. Germany, Austria and Switzerland held 71,65M people on 481.097,9 km² (148,93 inhabitants/km²), closely followed by the United Kingdom and Ireland with 46,05M on 311.813,8 km² (147,68 inhabitants/km²) and Italy and Malta with 36,2M on 300.408,2 km² (120,5 inhabitants/km²). France and Benelux stood at 53,95M (87,71 inhabitants/km²), masking a sharp contrast between densely packed Belgium and the Netherlands and France's thinly populated rural south and centre. Across the eastern and southern peripheries, Poland held 27,2M (88,18 inhabitants/km²), Czechoslovakia and Hungary 21,4M (97,92 inhabitants/km²), Romania, Bulgaria and Moldova 19,1M (50,97 inhabitants/km²), Yugoslavia, Albania, Greece and Eastern Thrace 20,1M (46,21 inhabitants/km²) and Spain, Portugal and the Atlantic islands 26,45M (44,47 inhabitants/km²). At the northern fringe, the Nordics and Baltic States counted 20,35M across 1.330.239,7 km² (15,3 inhabitants/km²), while Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland held 121k people scattered along the margins of 2.178.792,8 km² of ocean-bound tundra and ice.

## The First World War and the 1918–1919 Influenza Pandemic

The four years of industrialised warfare from August 1914 to November 1918 inflicted the first continental-scale mortality shock since the Napoleonic era, concentrated overwhelmingly on young adult males born between 1885 and 1900. Outside Russia, European combatant armies lost approximately 6,5M to 7M military dead: roughly 2M German soldiers, 1,4M French, 1,1M Austro-Hungarian, 880k British and Empire troops (over 720k from the United Kingdom and Ireland), 650k Italian, 330k Romanian, 275k to 370k Serbian and nearly 90k Bulgarian [@Mitchell2007; @Dupaquier1988]. Civilian excess mortality compounded military losses across occupied Belgium, northern France, Poland, Serbia and blockaded Germany and Austria-Hungary, where food rationing and fuel shortages pushed up tuberculosis and infant death rates. Wartime mobilisation also depressed births by 35% to 50% across belligerent countries, creating deep "hollow cohorts" whose demographic echo reappeared twenty years later when those shrunken generations reached marriageable age in the late 1930s.

Before demobilisation was even half finished, the 1918–1919 influenza pandemic struck belligerents and neutrals alike in three lethal waves between spring 1918 and spring 1919. Unlike ordinary seasonal influenza, the H1N1 strain killed disproportionately among young adults aged 20 to 40, amplifying the exact age-group losses already wrought by trench warfare. Across Europe outside Russia the pandemic claimed roughly 2M to 2,5M lives, hitting southern and peripheral states with particular ferocity: Spain lost an estimated 260k to 300k inhabitants, Italy 390k to 600k, Germany around 300k, France 240k, Britain 228k and Portugal over 60k to 135k. Local archival studies confirm that transport corridors, rail hubs and peri-urban marketplaces governed epidemic diffusion; in Malta, for example, suburban settlements linked by railway and market traffic suffered a measurable mortality penalty compared with isolated rural parishes, aggravated by concurrent measles outbreaks [@Tripp2023Emergence].

Despite these twin blows, aggregate European population across the 11 sub-regions edged upward slightly from 342,57M in 1914 to 348,81M in 1920 and 349,99M in 1921 (+2,2% over seven years), because neutral states (Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Switzerland) continued growing and post-armistice marriage booms lifted births sharply in 1920–1921. Only two sub-regions experienced net contraction across 1914–1921: France and Benelux (-0,3%, from 53,95M to 53,8M, reflecting France's devastating losses) and Poland (-0,1%, from 27,2M to 27,18M, battered successively by Eastern Front campaigns, typhus, famine and the Polish-Soviet War of 1919–1921).

## Post-Imperial Borders, Minority Treaties and Population Exchanges

The collapse of the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires redrew the political map of central and eastern Europe under the treaties of Versailles (1919), Saint-Germain (1919), Neuilly (1919), Trianon (1920), Riga (1921) and Lausanne (1923). Border revisions did not alter the fixed geographical sub-regional masks used in MAGNETIC, but they triggered massive cross-border migrations of officials, soldiers, refugees and ethnic minorities [@RosesWolf2019; @Okolski2021Migration]. Germany ceded Alsace-Lorraine to France (bringing 1,7M residents back under the French census from 1921), Posen, West Prussia and part of Upper Silesia to Poland, Eupen-Malmedy to Belgium and Northern Schleswig to Denmark; roughly 800k to 1M ethnic Germans migrated westward from Polish-administered territories into the Weimar Republic during the early 1920s. The Treaty of Trianon reduced Hungary to less than one-third of its pre-war territory and roughly 8M inhabitants, leaving more than 3M ethnic Hungarians inside Romania (Transylvania), Czechoslovakia (southern Slovakia and Subcarpathian Ruthenia) and Yugoslavia (Vojvodina), and driving roughly 350k to 400k Hungarian refugees into rump Hungary [@KSHHungary2024; @Vasiliev2022Hungarian].

In south-eastern Europe, border redrawing culminated in state-sponsored compulsory population transfer. Following the Greco-Turkish War of 1919–1922 and the burning of Smyrna, the Convention of Lausanne (January 1923) mandated the permanent exchange of Orthodox Christians from Anatolia and Eastern Thrace against Muslims from Greece (exempting Istanbul's Greeks and Western Thrace's Muslims). Roughly 1,2M to 1,3M Greek refugees poured into a Greek state of barely 5M inhabitants, transforming Macedonia, Western Thrace and the urban periphery of Athens and Piraeus, while 350k to 400k Muslims departed for Turkey [@StatBalkans2024]. Parallel voluntary and semi-compulsory exchanges between Bulgaria and Greece under the Treaty of Neuilly moved another 150k people across the Rhodope frontier. Meanwhile, Bessarabia's union with Greater Romania reshaped demographic and urban life along the Dniester and Prut valleys, as documented in the landmark Romanian census of 29 December 1930 [@Enciu2023Municipality; @Cojocaru2024Turkish].

## Inter-War Fertility Decline, the Great Depression and the Spanish Civil War

Between 1921 and 1939 European population grew by 46,37M (+13,3%) to reach 396,37M, yet growth rates diverged sharply between north-west and south-east. Across Sweden, Germany, Austria, England and Wales, France, Belgium and Switzerland, total fertility fell below replacement level during the Great Depression of 1929–1935 [@CoaleWatkins1986; @ONS2024; @BFS2024]. United States immigration quotas enacted in 1921 and 1924 closed the principal transatlantic safety valve that had absorbed millions of Italian, Polish, Irish, Greek and Iberian emigrants prior to 1914. Trapped inside Europe during an era of industrial slump, surplus agrarian workers moved into domestic capitals—Milan, Rome, Madrid, Warsaw, Budapest, Bucharest and Sofia—or migrated to labour-short France, which absorbed over 2M Italian, Polish, Belgian and Spanish immigrants during the 1920s [@INSEE2024; @Okolski2021Migration].

In the Iberian Peninsula, demographic expansion was brutally interrupted by the Spanish Civil War (July 1936 to April 1939). Combat casualties, Nationalist and Republican rear-guard executions, aerial bombardment of cities such as Guernica, Madrid and Barcelona, wartime malnutrition and epidemic typhus produced approximately 500k excess deaths, accompanied by a sharp birth deficit of roughly 450k to 500k unborn children [@INE2024]. Between January and February 1939, during the fall of Catalonia, nearly 450k to 500k Republican soldiers and civilians crossed the Pyrenees into French internment camps; although roughly half eventually returned, between 200k and 250k Spaniards remained permanently in exile in France, Mexico and the Americas. Even so, Spain's high inter-war birth rate and its subsequent non-belligerency during the Second World War allowed Spain, Portugal and the Atlantic islands to expand from 26,45M in 1914 to 33,2M in 1939 and 35,1M in 1945 (+32,7%).

## The Second World War, the Holocaust and 1945 Population Transfers

The Second World War (1939–1945) shattered the demographic trajectory of central, eastern and south-eastern Europe on a scale eclipsing even 1914–1918. Unlike the First World War, civilian deaths outnumbered military deaths across occupied Europe. Military casualties outside the Soviet Union included roughly 4,5M to 5,3M German and Austrian servicemen, 384k British, 300k to 350k Italian, 300k Romanian, 200k to 300k Hungarian, 210k French, 240k Polish, 95k Finnish and over 300k Yugoslav partisans and regulars [@Mitchell2007; @ONS2024; @GUSPoland2024]. Strategic bombing devastated German urban cores—Hamburg, Dresden, Cologne, Berlin and the Ruhr—killing over 400k German civilians, while British cities suffered roughly 60k Blitz fatalities and Dutch cities endured the Hongerwinter famine of 1944–1945 (~20k starvation deaths). In Greece, Axis requisitions and naval blockade triggered the Great Famine of 1941–1942, claiming roughly 300k lives.

At the centre of the civilian catastrophe stood the Holocaust: the systematic murder of approximately 6M European Jews by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1941 and 1945, alongside hundreds of thousands of Roma and Sinti, disabled patients and Soviet prisoners of war. Outside Soviet pre-1939 borders, Jewish destruction reached near-totality across Poland (~3M murdered, roughly 90% of pre-war Polish Jewry), Hungary (~550k–565k killed chiefly in the deportations of May–July 1944), Lithuania (~195k–210k, over 90%), Latvia (~70k, ~75%), Romania and Transnistria (~280k–380k), Czechoslovakia (~260k–277k), Germany and Austria (~200k–210k), the Netherlands (~102k, ~75%), France (~76k), Greece (~60k–67k, over 80%, wiping out Sephardic Thessaloniki), Yugoslavia (~60k–65k) and Belgium (~25k–29k) [@GUSPoland2024; @KSHHungary2024; @StatBaltics2024]. Small pre-war Jewish migrations to Mandatory Palestine (Yishuv) saved a fraction of central and eastern European communities prior to 1939 [@Dumitrescu2019State], while cohort follow-up of Holocaust survivors has later documented stark selective survival effects among those who endured extreme genocidal trauma [@Sagischwartz2013Against]. Roma communities across central and south-eastern Europe suffered parallel persecution, whereas Finland's small Roma minority remained outside German extermination zones [@Roman2020Christian].

In the closing months of 1944 and throughout 1945, Soviet westward advances and Allied decisions at Yalta and Potsdam unleashed the largest forced population transfer in European history. Poland's borders were shifted roughly 200 kilometres westward: the Soviet Union annexed the eastern Kresy east of the Curzon Line, while Poland received the former German territories east of the Oder-Neisse line (southern East Prussia, Pomerania, eastern Brandenburg and Silesia). Between late 1944 and 1945 millions of ethnic Germans fled or were expelled from East Prussia, Pomerania, Silesia, Danzig and the Czechoslovak Sudetenland (with expulsions continuing through 1946–1948 to reach roughly 12M total expellees), while over 1,5M Poles were repatriated from the Soviet-annexed east into the newly acquired western territories [@Okolski2021Migration; @GUSPoland2024]. Finland likewise evacuated 420k Karelians permanently inside its post-1944 borders. Because the 1945 benchmark captures Europe immediately after surrender—when millions were displaced, missing, in prisoner-of-war camps or mid-expulsion—the sub-regional drop of 11,63M between 1939 and 1945 reflects both direct mortality and the initial spatial redistribution of borders and peoples.

# Methodology

## Fixed Sub-Regional Geometry and Temporal Anchors

MAGNETIC partitions Europe outside the Soviet Union (plus Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland) into 11 fixed, mutually exclusive sub-regions totalling 7.148.884,3 km². Holding sub-regional polygons invariant between 1914 and 1945 prevents political border changes—such as the dissolution of Austria-Hungary, the re-establishment of Poland, the annexation of Alsace-Lorraine, the partition of Ireland or the 1945 shift to the Oder-Neisse line—from creating illusory demographic jumps in regional sums. Where historical national censuses changed territorial scope (notably Germany between 1910, 1925 and 1939; Poland between 1921, 1931 and 1946; Italy between 1911, 1921 and 1936; Romania between 1912 and 1930), census totals are adjusted to constant sub-regional boundaries using sub-administrative historical GIS polygons and published inter-censal boundary concordances [@Mitchell2007; @RosesWolf2019].

Six chronological benchmark horizons govern this chapter: 1914 (pre-war peak), 1920 and 1921 (immediate post-First World War and post-influenza census wave), 1925 (mid-inter-war stabilisation, anchored by the 1925 Weimar German census), 1939 (eve of the Second World War, anchored by the May 1939 German census and pre-war national registers) and 1945 (end of hostilities in Europe). Raw archival totals are anchored at the primary national census benchmarks available for each sub-region (for instance, 1914, 1921, 1939 and 1945 in the United Kingdom and Ireland, France and Benelux, Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary and Italy and Malta; 1914, 1920, 1939 and 1945 in Spain and Portugal; 1914, 1925, 1939 and 1945 in Germany, Austria and Switzerland, the Nordics and Baltics, the Balkans and the North Atlantic), with intermediate horizons interpolated consistently across the six-year series.

## Scraped Inter-War Historical GIS Sub-Administrative Enumerations

A defining strength of MAGNETIC for the twentieth century is its direct ingestion of sub-administrative historical GIS enumerations rather than reliance on national aggregates alone. For Chapter 18, 1.875 scraped sub-administrative and state-level historical GIS rows were compiled across three canonical inter-war snapshot regimes—1920, 1930 and 1940—drawing on 11 institutional statistical archives [@INSEE2024; @DEMOPAST2023; @INE2024; @Riksarkivet2023; @CSOIreland2023; @ONS2024; @BFS2024; @HGISGermany2014; @StatGL2024]. These series link official census counts directly to contemporaneous administrative geometry: the 90 inter-war French départements (restored with Moselle, Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin after Versailles), 69 to 91 Italian provinces across the 1921, 1931 and 1936 DEMOPAST and ISTAT censuses, 41 United Kingdom historic counties, 26 Irish Free State counties from the CSO CNA13 register, 51 Spanish historic provinces established under the 1833 Javier de Burgos decree, 18 Portuguese mainland distritos, 25 Swiss cantons, 11 Dutch historic provinces, 24 Swedish län from Riksarkivet and SCB, the Greenlandic North Atlantic census polygon and 13 central, northern and south-eastern European state polygons from CShapes (1920, 1930 and 1937 boundaries) matched to national censuses.

Table 1 summarises the exact unit counts and population sums across all 11 scraped historical GIS regimes for the 1920, 1930 and 1940 inter-war snapshots. Together, these sub-administrative polygons directly account for 292,71M inhabitants in 1920 (83,9% of the chapter total), 316,71M in 1930 and 337,54M in 1940 (85,2% of the 1939 pre-war total), with the remainder supplied by national censuses for Nordic, Baltic and Balkan states outside the CShapes subset.

Notice the administrative granularity preserved across snapshots. Italy's DEMOPAST provincial series expands from 69 provinces in 1921 (36,91M) to 89 provinces in 1931 (40,78M) and 91 provinces in 1936 (43,95M), registering both the post-First World War incorporation of Trentino-Alto Adige and Venezia Giulia and the Fascist regime's 1927 creation of 17 new provinces alongside reclaimed Agro Pontino districts [@DEMOPAST2023]. Across the Netherlands, 11 constant historic provinces surge by 31,3% from 6,81M in 1920 to 8,94M in 1940—the fastest two-decade demographic expansion in north-western Europe [@BFS2024]. By contrast, the 26 historic counties of the Irish Free State decline gently from 3,04M in 1920 to 2,97M in 1930 and 2,96M in 1940 as rural emigration to Britain and North America persisted after partition [@CSOIreland2023].

## Settlement Gazetteer Integration and Urban Disaggregation

Point-level spatial anchoring is supplied by a 10.023-settlement urban gazetteer spanning 45 modern European and North Atlantic states and territories. Primary institutional sources account for 86,01% (8.641 records) of the inventory: Buringh's long-run European urban series (1.391 cities), national statistical censuses across 29 countries led by Germany (1.129), France via INSEE (1.007), the United Kingdom (800), Spain via INE (703), Finland (466), Poland (319), Norway (265), Belgium (214) and the Netherlands (207), plus Eurostat's Urban Audit (613 metropolitan entities) and DEMOPAST Italian city records [@INSEE2024; @INE2024; @Eurostat2024; @ONS2024; @GUSPoland2024]. The remaining 1.405 records (13,98%) originate from the GeoNames municipal gazetteer supplement to fill small-town coverage across southern, Alpine and Balkan districts. Following the two-stage architecture of MAGNETIC, regional totals are derived strictly from national and sub-administrative census aggregates, while settlement coordinates and population series govern intra-regional spatial weighting and rank-size urban hierarchy analysis [@DeVries1984].

The correspondence between sub-administrative enumerations and fixed-mask sub-regional sums is tight and instructive. Germany on CShapes 1937 Weimar boundaries climbs from 60,89M in 1920 to 65,08M in 1930 and 69,31M in 1940 (158,2 inhabitants/km²); adding Austria (6,71M in 1940) and the 25 Swiss cantons (4,47M in 1940) yields 80,49M, matching MAGNETIC's 1939 Germany, Austria and Switzerland total (80,15M) within 0,4%. Likewise, combining the 41 UK historic counties (47,92M in 1940) with the 26 Irish Free State counties (2,96M in 1940) and Northern Ireland (~1,28M) reconciles directly with the United Kingdom and Ireland sub-regional curve (50,75M in 1939 rising to 52,18M in 1945) [@ONS2024; @CSOIreland2023].

At the metropolitan scale, Table 2 highlights the extraordinary spatial concentration of industrial Europe. Département 75 (Seine, encompassing Paris and its inner ring) packed 5,37M residents onto 1.140 km² by 1940—a density of 4.710,3 inhabitants/km² [@INSEE2024]. Middlesex and London held 5,82M across 2.466 km² (2.359,7 inhabitants/km²), while industrial Lancashire reached 5,07M on 5.150 km² (985,3 inhabitants/km²) [@ONS2024]. Outside western Europe, Greece's CShapes series jumps from 6,39M in 1930 to 7,35M in 1940 (+15% in a single decade) as the children of the 1923 Lausanne refugees entered adulthood, while Bulgaria expands from 5,73M to 6,34M (+10,7%) and Hungary from 7,98M in 1920 to 9,32M in 1940 (+16,7%) [@KSHHungary2024; @StatBalkans2024].

## Reconciliation of Wartime Mortality and Census Jumps

A second validation test checks whether net sub-regional changes between 1939 and 1945 are arithmetically consistent with established wartime casualty and migration balances. Across all 11 sub-regions, total population declined by 11,63M between 1939 (396,37M) and 1945 (384,74M). Adding the foregone six-year natural increase that Europe would have achieved at its late-1930s growth rate (~0,65% per year, or roughly +15,5M births over deaths) implies an aggregate demographic deficit of roughly 27M across Europe outside the USSR—comprising military deaths, civilian war deaths, Holocaust victims, wartime birth deficits and net outward displacement into the Soviet Union and overseas.

Sub-regional balances pass this accounting test individually:

- **Poland (-8,17M, -25,5% across 1939–1945)**: Pre-war population on the fixed sub-regional mask stood at 32,1M in 1939 and fell to 23,93M in 1945 (aligning closely with Poland's February 1946 census of 23,93M on post-Potsdam borders) [@GUSPoland2024]. This 8,17M drop reflects approximately 5,5M to 6M Polish wartime deaths (including ~3M Jews murdered in extermination camps and ghettos), plus the net difference between roughly 4M to 5M former eastern Kresy residents remaining in the USSR and the staggered flight and expulsion of ethnic Germans from the newly transferred Oder-Neisse territories [@Okolski2021Migration].
- **Germany, Austria and Switzerland (-3,3M, -4,1% across 1939–1945)**: Despite ~4,5M to 5,3M German and Austrian military deaths, >400k air-raid fatalities and >200k German and Austrian Jewish victims, the net 1945 headcount (76,85M) fell by only 3,3M below 1939 (80,15M) because natural increase remained positive during 1939–1943, neutral Switzerland expanded steadily and the first wave of ethnic German refugees from East Prussia, Pomerania, Silesia and the Sudetenland had already entered occupied Germany and Austria by mid-1945.
- **Czechoslovakia and Hungary (-2,55M, -10,7% across 1939–1945)**: Contraction from 23,8M to 21,25M captures roughly 850k to 950k Hungarian and Czechoslovak military, civilian and Holocaust deaths (including ~550k–565k Hungarian Jews and ~260k Czechoslovak Jews), the Soviet annexation of Subcarpathian Ruthenia (~700k–800k inhabitants) and the first phase of Sudeten German flight and expulsion in 1945 [@KSHHungary2024].
- **France and Benelux (-1,3M, -2,2% across 1939–1945)**: Falling from 59,25M to 57,95M reflects ~550k to 600k French military and civilian deaths, ~200k–250k Dutch and Belgian war and Holocaust deaths, hundreds of thousands of French prisoners of war and forced labourers still awaiting repatriation in May 1945 and depressed wartime fertility across France and Belgium [@INSEE2024; @Dupaquier1988].
- **Yugoslavia, Albania, Greece and Eastern Thrace (-850k, -3,3% across 1939–1945)**: Falling from 25,8M to 24,95M absorbs ~1M Yugoslav wartime dead and ~400k–500k Greek famine, reprisal and Holocaust dead, partly offset by persistently high rural birth rates in Albania, Macedonia, Kosovo and southern Yugoslavia [@StatBalkans2024].

# Results

## Continental Demographic Trajectory, 1914–1945

Across the 31 years from 1914 to 1945, European population outside the Soviet Union followed a distinct three-phase curve, plotted in Figure 1: sluggish wartime stagnation from 1914 to 1921 (+2,2%, adding 7,42M), steady inter-war expansion from 1921 to 1939 (+13,3%, adding 46,37M to reach 396,37M) and sharp Second World War contraction from 1939 to 1945 (-2,9%, losing 11,63M to finish at 384,74M). Measured end-to-end across 1914–1945, the 11 sub-regions added 42,17M inhabitants (+12,3%), equivalent to a compound annual growth rate of only 0,37% per year—less than half the pace of the late nineteenth century and a stark indicator of how profoundly two world wars retarded twentieth-century European growth [@Mitchell2007; @Atance2024Convergence].

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:world_wars_trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_magnetic/1.0-world-wars-and-interwar-europe/world_wars_and_interwar_europe_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:world_wars_trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Sub-regional and aggregate population trajectories across the 11 European and North Atlantic sub-regions from 1914 to 1945.</figcaption>
</figure>

Table 3 presents the sub-regional headcounts at the key benchmark horizons alongside inter-war (1914–1939) and Second World War (1939–1945) percentage shifts. Every single sub-region expanded between 1914 and 1939, ranging from +9,8% in France and Benelux and +10,2% in the United Kingdom and Ireland to +28,3% in Romania, Bulgaria and Moldova, +28,4% in Yugoslavia, Albania, Greece and Eastern Thrace and +36,4% in the North Atlantic. Between 1939 and 1945, however, Europe split cleanly into two demographic hemispheres: six sub-regions across Central, Eastern, Balkan, Baltic and occupied Western Europe suffered net population loss totalling -16,57M, while five insular, neutral or less severely depopulated sub-regions—Spain and Portugal (+1,9M), the United Kingdom and Ireland (+1,43M), Italy and Malta (+1,3M), Romania, Bulgaria and Moldova (+300k) and the North Atlantic (+15k)—gained +4,95M combined.

## Sub-Regional Demographic Narratives

### Western and North-Western Europe

The United Kingdom and Ireland rose smoothly from 46,05M in 1914 to 47,12M in 1921, 50,75M in 1939 and 52,18M in 1945 (+13,3% overall), overtaking Germany, Austria and Switzerland in 1945 to become Europe's most densely settled sub-region at 167,34 inhabitants/km² [@ONS2024]. Insular geography spared Britain land invasion and civilian famine during both conflicts; military losses in the Second World War (~384k) were roughly half those of 1914–1918, and a wartime rebound in births after 1942 pushed Britain's population upward even during the Blitz. Within the archipelago, however, demographic paths diverged sharply: England and Wales expanded steadily while the 26 counties of the Irish Free State declined from 3,04M in 1920 to 2,96M in 1940 under continuing emigration and late marriage [@CSOIreland2023].

France and Benelux exhibited the classic demographic signature of low-fertility Western Europe scarred by two invasions. Starting at 53,95M in 1914, the sub-region dipped to 53,8M in 1921 as France absorbed 1,4M military dead and a wartime deficit of roughly 1,4M births—losses only partially masked by the return of Alsace-Lorraine and steady growth in the neutral Netherlands [@Dupaquier1988; @INSEE2024]. Large-scale labour immigration into France and booming Dutch fertility lifted the sub-region to 59,25M by 1939 (+10,1% over 1921), before the 1940 defeat, German occupation, the deportation of 76k French Jews, 102k Dutch Jews and 25k–29k Belgian Jews, forced labour drafts and the Dutch Hongerwinter cut the 1945 total back to 57,95M (-2,2%).

### Central Europe: The German Sphere, Poland and the Danubian Basin

Germany, Austria and Switzerland remained Europe's single largest demographic block throughout the period, climbing from 71,65M in 1914 (20,9% of the chapter total) to 73,2M in 1925 and 80,15M in 1939 (+11,9%), before dropping to 76,85M in 1945 (-4,1%, 20% of the chapter total). Weimar Germany's marital fertility plummeted during the 1920s and early 1930s, briefly rebounding after 1933 under Nazi pronatalist marriage loans and economic recovery [@CoaleWatkins1986]. Austria stagnated around 6,5M to 6,7M throughout the inter-war decades as Vienna—once the capital of a 52M empire—shrank into an oversized metropolis inside a small Alpine republic. Switzerland grew steadily from 3,9M in 1920 to 4,47M in 1940 under armed neutrality [@BFS2024]. Between 1939 and 1945, war mortality across the Reich—concentrated overwhelmingly on the Eastern Front after 1941—killed nearly 5M German and Austrian men in uniform and over 400k civilians in bombed cities, stripping Germany's age pyramid of young men for half a century.

Poland suffered the gravest demographic catastrophe of any European sub-region. Already stagnant between 1914 (27,2M) and 1921 (27,18M) after seven years of shifting front lines and epidemics, the Second Polish Republic rebounded vigorously during the inter-war years to reach 32,1M by 1939 (+18,1% over 1921), sustained by high rural birth rates in Galicia and the eastern provinces [@GUSPoland2024]. Between September 1939 and May 1945 that entire inter-war gain was obliterated and pushed 3,27M below its 1914 starting point, plunging to 23,93M (-25,5% in six years). Roughly one in six pre-war Polish citizens died—including 90% of Europe's largest Jewish community—while Warsaw was systematically razed after the 1944 Uprising and post-war border changes uprooted millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Belarusians and Germans simultaneously [@Okolski2021Migration].

Czechoslovakia and Hungary followed a parallel, slightly muted trajectory, growing from 21,4M in 1914 to 21,6M in 1921 and 23,8M in 1939 (+11,2%) before contracting by 2,55M (-10,7%) to 21,25M in 1945. Bohemia and Moravia already displayed western European low fertility during the 1930s, whereas Slovakia and agrarian Hungary sustained moderate natural increase [@KSHHungary2024]. The late-war catastrophe fell with appalling speed: between May and July 1944, following the German occupation of Hungary, over 437k Hungarian Jews were deported to Auschwitz in eight weeks, lifting total Hungarian and Czechoslovak Holocaust deaths above 800k, followed by the siege of Budapest, Soviet annexation of Subcarpathian Ruthenia and the start of the Sudeten German expulsion in spring 1945.

### Southern Europe: Italy, Iberia and the Balkans

Italy and Malta climbed continuously from 36,2M in 1914 to 38,1M in 1921 (+5,2%), 44,1M in 1939 (+21,8% over 1914) and 45,4M in 1945 (+25,4% overall), raising density from 120,5 to 151,13 inhabitants/km² [@DEMOPAST2023]. Even though Italy lost ~650k soldiers in the First World War, ~400k to 600k civilians to 1918–1919 influenza and ~450k to 500k soldiers and civilians in 1940–1945, the sudden closure of transatlantic emigration after 1924 trapped southern Italian natural increase inside the peninsula and fuelled rapid urban growth in Rome, Milan, Turin and Naples.

Spain, Portugal and the Atlantic islands recorded the strongest continuous expansion on the European mainland, rising from 26,45M in 1914 to 27,4M in 1920, 33,2M in 1939 and 35,1M in 1945 (+32,7% overall, +5,7% across 1939–1945) [@INE2024]. Neutrality in both world wars shielded Iberia from continental industrial slaughter, though the 1918–1919 influenza pandemic and the 1936–1939 Spanish Civil War inflicted severe internal scars: Spain's 1940 provincial census (25,96M) stood roughly one million people below its pre-war demographic trendline owing to Civil War mortality, Republican exile and the 1937–1939 birth trough.

In south-eastern Europe, Romania, Bulgaria and Moldova surged from 19,1M in 1914 to 20,9M in 1925, 24,5M in 1939 (+28,3%) and 24,8M in 1945 (+29,8% overall) [@StatBalkans2024]. Yugoslavia, Albania, Greece and Eastern Thrace grew almost identically across the inter-war years—from 20,1M in 1914 to 25,8M in 1939 (+28,4%), boosted by the 1923 Lausanne refugee influx into Greece—before plunging by 850k (-3,3%) to 24,95M in 1945 under Axis occupation, Ustaša mass murder, partisan civil war, the Greek Great Famine and the destruction of Yugoslav and Greek Jewry.

### Northern Europe and the North Atlantic

The Nordics and Baltic States grew modestly from 20,35M in 1914 to 20,95M in 1925 and 22,55M in 1939 (+10,8%) before dipping to 22,15M in 1945 (-1,8%). That mild aggregate decline conceals a stark east-west split across the Baltic Sea. Sweden (rising from 5,82M in 1920 to 6,55M in 1940 via Riksarkivet and SCB), Denmark and Norway maintained positive natural increase throughout the Second World War [@Riksarkivet2023]. By contrast, Finland absorbed heavy military casualties in the Winter War (1939–1940) and Continuation War (1941–1944) alongside the evacuation of 420k Karelians, while Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania suffered demographic devastation—losing 15% to 25% of their pre-war residents through the 1940–1941 Soviet deportations, the Holocaust (which annihilated over 90% of Lithuanian Jewry and three-quarters of Latvian Jewry), Baltic German repatriation (Umsiedlung), wartime conscription and the autumn 1944 flight of over 200k Baltic refugees to Sweden and Germany [@StatBaltics2024].

Finally, Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Greenland expanded faster in proportional terms than any other sub-region, growing by 48,8% from 121k in 1914 to 136k in 1925, 165k in 1939 and 180k in 1945 [@Hagstofa2024; @StatGL2024]. Insulated from front-line combat and rapidly modernising their fisheries and public health systems, Iceland and the Faroes achieved dramatic reductions in infant and tuberculosis mortality, while Greenland's coastal settlements grew steadily from 14,4k in 1920 to 19k in 1940.

## Density Shifts and Urban Hierarchy

Table 4 tracks population density and continental shares from 1914 to 1945. The centre of demographic gravity shifted measurably away from war-torn Central and Eastern Europe toward Western and Southern Europe. Between 1914 and 1945 Poland's share of the chapter total fell from 7,9% to 6,2%, Czechoslovakia and Hungary dropped from 6,2% to 5,5% and Germany, Austria and Switzerland eased from 20,9% to 20%, whereas Italy and Malta climbed from 10,6% to 11,8%, Spain and Portugal from 7,7% to 9,1% and the two Balkan sub-regions combined from 11,4% to 12,9%.

Urbanisation accelerated markedly throughout the inter-war era despite industrial recessions, producing the dense metropolitan hierarchy depicted in Figure 2. Greater London dominated Europe throughout the period, expanding from 6,72M in 1914 to 7,95M by 1945, followed by Greater Paris (3,94M in 1914, peaking at 4,46M in 1940) and Berlin (rising strongly following the 1920 Greater Berlin municipal unification). Secondary capitals and industrial agglomerations—Milan, Madrid, Barcelona, Naples, Rome, Athens, Vienna, Budapest, Bucharest, Hamburg, Lisbon, Warsaw, Glasgow, Birmingham, Prague, Stockholm, Lyon, Marseille, Munich, Copenhagen and Sofia—all crossed or approached the million mark in metropolitan extent during the inter-war years [@Eurostat2024; @RosesWolf2019]. Only Istanbul (in Turkey-in-Europe) contracted steadily across the chapter's settlement series, slipping from 1,1M in 1914 to 998,5k by 1945 after losing its imperial capital status to Ankara in 1923 and shedding much of its Greek and Armenian commercial bourgeoisie.

# Limitations

Four structural limitations govern historical demography for the 1914–1945 window and must be kept clearly in view when interpreting these figures.

First, **the 1945 endpoint captures Europe in mid-upheaval rather than post-war equilibrium**. No national census could be taken in Germany, Poland, Austria, Yugoslavia or Hungary in May 1945. Millions of soldiers remained in Allied and Soviet prisoner-of-war camps while millions of forced labourers (Ostarbeiter) and displaced persons awaited repatriation across occupied Germany; meanwhile, the main wave of ethnic German expulsions from Silesia, Pomerania, East Prussia and the Sudetenland extended through 1946–1948. The 1945 benchmark therefore interpolates carefully between 1939 pre-war registers and the first post-war censuses of 1946 (France, Germany, Poland), 1947 (Netherlands, Belgium, Czechoslovakia) and 1948 (Yugoslavia, Romania) [@GUSPoland2024; @StatBalkans2024; @INSEE2024].

Second, **fixed sub-regional masks obscure severe intra-regional divergences where wartime frontiers cut through a single polygon**. Grouping the neutral Nordic democracies with the Soviet- and German-occupied Baltic States inside a single Nordics and Baltic States sub-region compresses catastrophic Baltic population losses (-15% to -25%) against steady Swedish, Danish and Norwegian growth into a deceptively gentle -1,8% sub-regional dip. Likewise, grouping Romania, Bulgaria and Moldova masks the devastating Holocaust in Bessarabia and Bukovina behind high rural Moldovan and Romanian birth rates. Users requiring national or provincial resolution should consult the underlying 1.149-row HGIS sub-administrative ledger rather than inferring homogeneity from sub-regional aggregates.

Third, **overlapping urban boundary definitions appear in the merged 10.046-settlement gazetteer**. Because MAGNETIC integrates Eurostat's Urban Audit (which back-casts modern Greater City and Functional Urban Area footprints) alongside historical municipal censuses (INSEE, ISTAT and DEMOPAST, Polish and German national censuses) and Buringh's long-run urban corpus, several major capitals appear both as wider metropolitan agglomerations and as strict municipal cores—for instance, Milan's back-cast greater city (2,74M in 1940) alongside its ISTAT municipal census counts (718,2k in 1921, 991,9k in 1931 and 1,12M in 1936), or dual municipal and metropolitan entries for Rome, Vienna, Budapest and Warsaw [@Eurostat2024; @DEMOPAST2023]. Furthermore, back-cast Eurostat series smooth over abrupt wartime demolitions such as Warsaw's destruction in 1944 or the bombing of German cities. Regional macro-totals are insulated from these boundary artefacts because they derive independently from census and HGIS aggregates rather than summed settlement rows.

Fourth, **minor crowdsourced supplementation remains necessary at the rural tail**. Although 86,01% of the 10.046 settlements come directly from official national statistical institutes and scholarly urban datasets, 1.405 smaller towns (13,98%) rely on the GeoNames municipal supplement, particularly in southern Italy, the western Balkans and micro-territories where pre-1945 municipal census digitisation remains patchy.

# Conclusion

The 31 years between 1914 and 1945 broke the momentum of modern European demographic expansion. Across 11 sub-regions covering 7.148.884,3 km², Europe outside the Soviet Union added 53,79M people between 1914 and 1939—rising from 342,57M to 396,37M despite First World War combat losses, the 1918–1919 influenza pandemic, the Spanish Civil War and deepening fertility decline—only to lose 11,63M inhabitants (-2,9%) during the six years of the Second World War, ending at 384,74M in 1945. No previous modern conflict had reshaped Europe's ethnic and spatial geography so violently: the Holocaust destroyed millennia-old Jewish communities across Poland, Hungary, Lithuania, Latvia, Romania, Czechoslovakia, Greece, Yugoslavia and the Netherlands; Poland lost a quarter of its population in six years; and the 1945 shift of borders to the Oder-Neisse and Curzon lines set in motion the largest forced population transfer in European history. Anchored by 1.149 scraped inter-war historical GIS sub-administrative enumerations and 10.046 geocoded settlements, these series establish the exact demographic baseline from which post-1945 reconstruction, the baby boom and the Cold War division of Europe unfolded.
